raw_case_text:
A 37-year-old male presented with on-and-off fever (102 degrees F) for four days and generalized weakness in both upper and lower limbs. All necessary investigations were performed. On evaluation, the patient was diagnosed with dengue fever with thrombocytopenia. On examination, the patient was conscious and coherent with the following vital signs: blood pressure of 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate of 54 bpm, and saturation of peripheral oxygen (Spo2) of 95%. Neurological examination revealed sensory loss below the T4 level with absent deep tendon reflexes. The patient had a Glasgow coma score (GCS) of 15 without any signs of meningeal irritation. The pupillary size and reaction were normal. Serological tests for malaria and typhoid infection were negative. He had a hematocrit of 46%, and thrombocytopenia (1.01 lakhs/cumm) with an increased total leukocyte count (19,400 cells/cumm) and a normal coagulation profile (prothrombin time (PT) 14.1 sec, international normalized ratio (INR) 1.2). The rest of the laboratory results were unremarkable.
The patient was started on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline 100mg), analgesics, and other supportive medications. His weakness gradually progressed with the inability to walk or stand. The patient was referred for a spine MRI, which showed long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage in the cervical and dorsal spine (up to D8 level) causing mild to moderate lateral compression and anterior displacement of the cord at these levels (Figures 1, 2). An MRI of the brain was also performed which revealed mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns of the lateral ventricles which correlated with CT (Figure 3). After the radiology report, a neurosurgeon was consulted regarding the MRI findings and explained the grave risk and poor prognosis in relation to the radiological findings. Since the epidural hemorrhage was a long-segment (cervicodorsal spine epidural hematoma from C2 to D7 level) and not focal, surgical treatment was not possible and conservative management was advised. The patient was intubated due to unresponsiveness on day 10 of the dengue fever diagnosis. On the same day, the patient's family members decided to have the patient discharged against medical advice. Subsequently, the patient died of the disease.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 37-year-old male presenting with intermittent fever (102 °F) and generalized weakness in all four extremities for four days.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: A 37-year-old male presented with a 4-day history of intermittent fever (102 °F) and progressive generalized weakness of both upper and lower limbs. On admission, he was alert and coherent but had sensory loss below T4 level and areflexia. Despite antibiotic and supportive therapy, neurological weakness rapidly progressed to complete paraplegia and inability to stand or walk, followed by unresponsiveness on day 10 requiring endotracheal intubation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Generalized weakness in all four limbs; sensory level loss below T4; absent deep tendon reflexes; absence of bowel/bladder details.

objective.physical_examination: Vitals: Blood pressure 180/100 mmHg, pulse rate 54 bpm (bradycardia), SpO2 95% on room air. Neurologic: GCS 15 initially, alert and coherent; pupils equal and reactive; absence of meningeal irritation. Sensory exam revealed sensory level loss below T4. Motor/Reflexes: Absent deep tendon reflexes in all limbs, with rapid progression to flaccid paralysis; subsequently deteriorated to unresponsiveness (day 10) requiring tracheal intubation.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hematocrit 46%, total leukocyte count 19,400 cells/cumm (leukocytosis), platelet count 1.01 lakhs/cumm (thrombocytopenia). Coagulation profile: PT 14.1 sec, INR 1.2 (normal). Infectious serology: Malaria smear and typhoid serology negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Whole spine MRI: Extensive, long-segment spinal epidural hemorrhage in the cervical and dorsal spine extending from C2 to D7/D8 level, causing mild-to-moderate lateral cord compression and anterior spinal cord displacement. Brain MRI and non-contrast CT: Mild diffuse subarachnoid hemorrhage with subtle dependent intraventricular hemorrhage in the bilateral occipital horns of the lateral ventricles.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Confirmed Dengue virus infection (dengue fever with thrombocytopenia) complicated by extensive non-traumatic long-segment cervicothoracic spinal epidural hematoma (C2 to D8), spinal cord compression, diffuse intracranial subarachnoid hemorrhage, and intraventricular hemorrhage. Malaria and typhoid were excluded.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on intravenous antibiotics (doxycycline 100 mg), analgesics, and supportive neurocritical therapy. Urgent neurosurgical consultation deemed surgical decompression unfeasible due to the extensive non-focal multi-segmental hematoma (C2-D7/D8) and grave operative risk; conservative management was advised. Due to progressive neurological deterioration and unresponsiveness, the patient was intubated for mechanical ventilation on hospital day 10. The family opted for discharge against medical advice, and the patient subsequently succumbed.
